title: EcoSentinel
speaker: Mario
cue: Point to the photograph, then pause after the question
speech: Suppose we upload this photograph and ask what the animal eats. Where should the answer come from? EcoSentinel connects the image to wildlife information that we can check. We will follow that path from the original file to a search result, and finally to an answer with sources.

title: A photograph starts the investigation
speaker: Mario
cue: The domain gives the pipeline a purpose
speech: That question matters outside a classroom too. A teacher preparing a wildlife lesson, or a field team reviewing an observation, may have a photograph but need a call recording or a habitat description. Those materials often sit in separate catalogues. We bring them together, using Iberian fauna as a clear and limited domain for the project.

title: Three modalities, one reference dataset
speaker: Mario
cue: Counts describe the reference installation
speech: To build that collection, we gathered one hundred images, thirty-four recordings and sixty-four texts for ten Iberian species. They come from Wikimedia, Xeno-canto, Wikipedia and GBIF. The sources do not cover every species equally. The lizard, for example, has no audio. We keep these gaps visible, and preserve source information so that users can check where each record came from.

title: The EcoSentinel pipeline
speaker: Mario
cue: Follow the boundaries and the source references
speech: The files pass through four zones. Landing preserves the originals, Formatted gives each type a common format, and Trusted checks quality and duplicates. Exploitation then creates search vectors. The first three zones use object storage, while Chroma stores the vectors on disk. Searches open a verified copy because Chroma can make internal writes when opened. We refresh this copy after data changes, without calculating embeddings again. The orchestrator connects all these stages in the order shown on the next slide.

title: The 16 steps in order
speaker: Mario
cue: Follow the six stage groups from top to bottom; do not read all names aloud
speech: These are the sixteen steps behind that diagram. We start by checking storage and creating any missing buckets. Then we ingest local files and verify their copies in Persistent. Three formatters and three validators handle images, audio and text. Five indexing steps build the collections, and the last step checks that accepted files and vector parts agree. Everything runs in sequence. A failure stops later steps, and a rerun checks what already completed. Optional acquisition adds three downloads after storage setup. We will now explain the decisions inside those stages.

title: Hashes and embeddings
speaker: Mario
cue: Explain why identity comes before model inference
speech: Before we look inside Landing, there is an important distinction between hashes and embeddings. At ingestion, we need to check file identity. SHA-two-fifty-six reads the bytes once in small blocks, without decoding the media or loading a neural model. That makes the check cheap and predictable, although we have not measured a speed ratio. An embedding answers a later question: whether content is related. Saving a photograph again can change its hash while leaving its meaning almost unchanged. We therefore use hashes for identity and integrity, then embeddings for similarity.

title: Landing: file identity and verified copies
speaker: Mario
cue: Copy, verify, then mark complete
speech: Landing turns that identity into an object key: the first sixteen hexadecimal characters of the hash, followed by the filename. On a rerun, we first look for that object in Temporal and check its source information. If it has already left Temporal, a completion record points to its copy in Persistent. We check that the target exists before skipping it. The copying step verifies the bytes before writing this record, so a broken copy cannot look complete. This proves completion of Landing; Trusted makes its own decision later.

title: Landing: four identity cases
speaker: Mario
cue: The filename is part of the submitted-file identity
speech: The filename in that key explains these four cases. Same bytes and same name reuse the existing record. Same bytes with a different name enter again because we preserve the identity of the submitted file, including its name. That costs some storage, but Trusted will check duplicate content later. Different bytes with the same name also enter, under a new hash, so they cannot overwrite the first version. When both change, we get a new record too. Landing handles simple identity checks before the more detailed quality work.

title: Formatted choices for wildlife data
speaker: Mario
cue: Connect every format choice to wildlife data
speech: Once the originals are safe, Formatted gives each type a common representation. For photographs, JPEG at quality ninety-five balances detail and file size. It is usually efficient for photos, but still loses information, so we keep the original and its dimensions. MPO needs special handling because one file can contain several photographs. We use its first photograph and preserve the others upstream. For audio, a faint call may sit behind rain, wind or other animals. FLAC avoids another lossy encoding step, while keeping background sound and quiet sections. Our sixteen-bit conversion can still reduce precision from richer sources. Finally, UTF-eight preserves Spanish and English text. For JSON, we first try recognised content fields and only fall back to the longest string when none is found. With the formats consistent, Sambhav will explain the quality decisions.

title: Trusted: rejection or warning?
speaker: Sambhav
cue: Separate hard failures from useful ecological variation
speech: Trusted decides whether a file is usable and which issues need a warning. Images must decode, stay below twenty megabytes and forty megapixels, and have at least one hundred and twenty-eight pixels on each side. We check pixels as well as bytes because a small compressed file can still need a lot of memory. Audio has a two-hundred-megabyte cap and text has four. These are practical budgets for our local system, rather than scientifically optimal thresholds. Hashes find exact duplicates. For similar images, a perceptual hash finds candidates, then we check structure and colour. Darkness, possible watermarks and quiet audio usually remain warnings, preserving material that may still be useful.

title: Quality decisions leave an audit trail
speaker: Sambhav
cue: Show the actual report and distinguish completeness from truth
speech: Those decisions need to be visible, so every checked asset gets a JSON quality record. We use the records to create an HTML report, CSV measurements and plots. Here is the actual image report. All one hundred reference images remain accepted, including thirty-two possible watermark warnings. Source fields are complete, which helps us trace the records. It does not prove that every source label is correct. The charts make the effects of our decisions easier to inspect.

title: Did filtering change species representation?
speaker: Sambhav
cue: Before and after measure the effect of our policy
speech: This chart compares species counts before and after Trusted. If a rule removed many images from one species, we would see that imbalance here. In our reference batch, both bars show ten images per species and the measured distribution change is zero. That tells us about the effect of our filtering on this selected dataset, rather than about animal populations in nature.

title: Quiet intervals remain in the evidence
speaker: Sambhav
cue: The warning has an explicit consequence
speech: Audio shows why a warning can be more useful than rejection. Nine recordings contain many quiet intervals, yet a distant animal call can itself be quiet. Removing those sections could also lose background context. We therefore keep all thirty-four recordings and record the warning for inspection. Once these quality decisions are recorded, the accepted material is ready for indexing.

title: Five collections, 6,021 embeddings
speaker: Sambhav
cue: Completeness is more than a row count
speech: A long recording or document needs several searchable segments. This is why one hundred and ninety-eight files produce six thousand and twenty-one embeddings across five collections. Each vector keeps its file identity, source and segment position. On a rerun, we check compatibility and the complete set of expected segments. Counting rows alone could miss a missing segment hidden by a duplicate. These checks let us repair incomplete work without calculating every vector again.

title: Three encoders, three relationships
speaker: Sambhav
cue: Model choice follows the retrieval relationship
speech: The five collections use three model families because the relationships are different. CLIP connects photographs with descriptions, while CLAP connects sounds with descriptions, including animal calls. Multilingual E-five small handles detailed Spanish and English text retrieval. All three run on CPU. Their outputs stay in compatible spaces: CLIP and CLAP may both produce five-hundred-and-twelve numbers, but the coordinates mean different things. When searching across models, we combine result positions rather than comparing raw scores. Inside each space, we use cosine similarity.

title: Similarity is an angle, not a probability
speaker: Sambhav
cue: The two-dimensional calculation illustrates the actual normalised-vector rule
speech: Cosine compares the directions of two vectors. We divide their dot product by their lengths. Since we normalise our vectors to unit length, the calculation becomes just the dot product. In this two-dimensional example, the candidates score zero point nine six, zero point six and zero. The first points closest to the query, while the last is perpendicular. Our real vectors have hundreds of components, but the same rule applies. The score describes closeness in that model space. It does not give a probability that the animals belong to the same species.

title: Finding neighbours: HNSW in Chroma
speaker: Sambhav
cue: Cosine scores a pair; HNSW selects neighbours through a layered graph
speech: Cosine scores a pair of vectors, but we also need a way to find good candidates. Chroma uses H-N-S-W, a graph with several levels. It makes large jumps at the upper levels and explores nearby candidates below. This saves a full scan for larger sets, but the search is approximate. When sixty-four or fewer vectors remain after filtering, our code compares every vector instead. We chose sixty-four as a small, bounded fallback for tiny collections that may lack a saved graph. It is a practical cap, not an optimum established by comparing thirty-two, sixty-four and one hundred and twenty-eight.

title: Task 1: a real image query
speaker: Sambhav
cue: Point out both the useful matches and the failure
speech: Here is what that search produces in Task one using real CLIP embeddings. We exclude the reference file and return each other file once. Four of these five results have a lynx label, while one has a wolf label. A cropped version also remains. The example shows useful visual matches, but also why we should not treat similarity as species identification or assume that every near duplicate has disappeared.

title: Task 2: one query, images and text
speaker: Sambhav
cue: One query returns different modalities
speech: Task two uses an aligned space to connect different types of files. Here, one text query returns four images and four texts. The displayed image scores zero point three three two. It can still be useful even though that score is lower than the image-to-image example, because query types have different score ranges. We reserve room for both modalities so that text chunks do not fill the list. Users can request one to fifty distinct files, with eight as the default. Wassim will now show how retrieved material supports a generated answer.

title: Task 3: answer from retrieved evidence
speaker: Wassim
cue: Same preparation in memory, no stored query
speech: Task three retrieves evidence before asking Qwen to answer. An uploaded image first receives the shared JPEG conversion in memory, without being stored. Quality issues produce warnings, while invalid files and resource limits stop the request. We reuse a stored Trusted image unchanged. CLIP then finds visual candidates, BLIP produces an automatic caption, and E-five retrieves text evidence. Qwen receives that selected text and its source identifiers, rather than image pixels. We check the returned quotations and references, while recognising that a correct quotation does not guarantee a correct interpretation.

title: The frog case: evidence and uncertainty
speaker: Wassim
cue: A candidate remains a hypothesis
speech: This recorded frog example shows that distinction. The answer describes habitat and diet using source quotations, while the candidate species remains a hypothesis about the photograph. When we asked for the complete genome instead, the system declined because the evidence was missing. These cases show how the model pipeline behaves, rather than measuring general accuracy. They were recorded before the query-preparation update. We use the saved examples in the talk because a fresh CPU response can take minutes.

title: The second run adds zero new vectors
speaker: Wassim
cue: The full CLI has been exercised twice
speech: Useful answers are only one part of the project. We also need a pipeline that can run again safely. In an earlier isolated CPU demonstration, three synthetic files produced seven vectors on the first run. The second run completed all sixteen steps and added zero new vectors. The final check confirmed that the stored files and vector parts agreed. The image was noise and the audio was a tone, so this tests repeat execution, rather than wildlife relevance.

title: How we tested the pipeline
speaker: Wassim
cue: Current offline evidence versus earlier native runs
speech: We test failure cases as well as successful runs. The current offline suite passes four hundred and sixty-nine tests. The latest additions check conflicting source records, missing copies, failed storage requests and incomplete vector sets. They verify that existing data stays intact. Query tests also compare prepared bytes with the actual Formatted output and check limits before conversion. Earlier integration and CPU runs provide separate evidence for real storage and models. Offline coverage is seventy-two point three seven percent of measured statements. We use it to find gaps, while the assertions tell us whether the expected behaviour holds.

title: An input can fail before it reaches storage
speaker: Wassim
cue: The executable header is harmless test data
speech: One concrete failure case is this file called lynx dot jpg, containing a harmless Windows executable header. The Security Gate blocks it before hashing or upload, and the test never executes it. Other cases cover corrupt files, empty inputs and oversized archives. Compare that with a possible watermark: we keep the image and warn the user because it may still contain useful wildlife information. These different outcomes reflect the purpose of each rule. The gate checks inputs; it does not replace antivirus.

title: A query with a traceable answer
speaker: Wassim
cue: Return to the opening question
speech: We began with a photograph and asked where the answer should come from. EcoSentinel makes that route inspectable, from the original file and its processing decisions to the retrieved sources. Our next evaluation needs expert-labelled queries, including useful questions that the system fails to answer. Thank you.
